classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a difference-of-squares factorisation to establish the supplied alternatives, then solve and combine the two branches.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Given the equation $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\cos2\theta$, show that $\tan\theta=-1$ or $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta+\cos\theta&=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta\\\sin\theta+\cos\theta&=(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)\\(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)(1-\cos\theta+\sin\theta)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Thus $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1$.
In the first branch, $\cos\theta\ne0$, since otherwise $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\pm1$. Dividing by $\cos\theta$ gives $\tan\theta=-1$.
Therefore $\tan\theta=-1$ or $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1$.

For $\tan\theta=-1$, $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.
For $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt2\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)&=1\\\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\end{aligned}$$
The transformed domain is $\dfrac\pi4\le\theta+\dfrac\pi4<\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\theta+\frac\pi4&=\frac\pi4,\frac{7\pi}{4}\\\theta&=0,\frac{3\pi}{2}.\end{aligned}$$
Combining both branches, $\theta=0,\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.
